title: Get safe drinking water
short: Store it, make it safer, keep it clean
intro: Readings for when the tap water stops or may not be safe: how much to keep, how to make water safer to drink, and how to keep it clean. The pages come from the WHO and from Swiss, German and Austrian civil protection.

choices.label: Tap water is off or might be unsafe
choices.hint: A flood, a broken pipe, a warning not to drink it

read.label: Why every home needs a water reserve
read.note: In German. A storm can damage a pipe or make tap water unsafe; keep a reserve until the supply is back.

read.label: What treating water at home can and cannot do
read.note: Only water for drinking and food needs treating, about 5 litres a person a day. These methods do not remove chemicals.

read.label: After a flood: before you drink from the tap
read.note: In Italian. Among the steps after a flood: check that no local notice forbids drinking tap water, and do not eat food the water touched.

choices.label: I can boil water
choices.hint: A gas stove, a camping stove, a fire

read.label: Boiling, chlorine and sunlight
read.note: Bring water to a rolling boil; it is effective but uses a lot of fuel. The page also covers chlorine and sun disinfection.

read.label: A simple filter, then boil the water
read.note: In German. An improvised sand filter for cloudy water, after which the water is boiled for about a minute.

choices.label: I have water tablets or chlorine
choices.hint: Tablets or drops from a pharmacy or a camping shop

read.label: Using chlorine tablets, step by step
read.note: A picture guide for clear and for dirty water, then a 30-minute wait. The dose depends on the product: follow its instructions.

read.label: What chlorine does, and what it does not
read.note: Chlorine kills most germs but not all; products differ in strength, so always use the maker's instructions.

read.label: Tablets, the bathtub, and the sun
read.note: In German. Disinfecting tablets from the pharmacy, filling the bathtub as a reserve, and sun disinfection in bottles.

choices.label: No fuel and no tablets
choices.hint: Only clear bottles, sunlight, cloth or sand

read.label: Let it settle, then filter it
read.note: Shaking for air, letting dirt settle, and household filters. Settled water still needs a proven treatment.

read.label: Sun disinfection in clear bottles (SODIS)
read.note: Clear one- or two-litre bottles of clear water in direct sun; how long depends on the sun and the bottle.

read.label: Sun disinfection, as an Austrian guide explains it
read.note: In German. Bottle size, how long to leave it in the sun, and how many germs it kills.

choices.label: How much water do we need?
choices.hint: Per person, per day, for how many days

read.label: About 2 litres a person a day
read.note: In German. Half a litre of it for cooking; how much a family of three needs for 3, 5 or 10 days; water for pets.

read.label: The least people need to survive, and for hygiene
read.note: Written for relief planners: litres a day to drink and eat, for washing and for cooking; a flushing toilet uses up to 7 litres.

read.label: Seven bottles a person for a week
read.note: In German. The Austrian rule of a week without shopping or power, and a yearly check of the stock.

choices.label: Store water and keep it clean
choices.hint: Bottles, jerrycans, buckets, how long it keeps

read.label: Bottled water, and keeping tap water for months
read.note: In German. Why water comes first, which bottled water keeps best, and storing tap water in very clean containers, dark and cool.

read.label: Keep treated water clean
read.note: Clean covered containers in a cool dark place, clean hands, and a tap on the container so no one dips into it.

choices.label: The power is out: will the water keep running?
choices.hint: A long power cut, the waterworks, the sewers

read.label: Waterworks need electricity
read.note: In German. Without power the water supply can stop; what else a long outage can disrupt.

read.label: First steps in a blackout: fill containers
read.note: In German. Check the stock, fill pots, buckets and bottles while water still runs, and use it sparingly.

limits.text: Treating water at home removes dirt and germs, but not chemicals.
Water that has been left to settle still needs a proven treatment before you drink it.
Chlorine does not kill every germ: some, such as cryptosporidium, resist it. Always follow the maker's instructions.
During a flood, do not drink tap water: it may be contaminated.
After a flood, drink tap water only once no local order or notice forbids it.
Diseases carried by dirty water, such as cholera or typhoid, can kill if they are not treated.
9 litres a person cover drinking and cooking for three days, not washing or flushing the toilet.

prepare.label: How much water to keep for 3, 5 or 10 days
At least 9 litres a person: one pack of six bottles
prepare.note: In German. Easy to carry and keeps for months.

prepare.label: A week's stock, checked once a year
Know where to turn off the water, and ask your town
prepare.note: In German. Also water for washing and flushing, not only for drinking.

learn.label: Emergency treatment of drinking water at the point of use
learn.note: WHO technical note (2013), written for relief workers: settling, filters, boiling, chlorine, sunlight, storage.

learn.label: How much water is needed in emergencies
learn.note: WHO technical note (2013) for relief planners.

learn.label: Supplies guide
learn.note: In German. Austrian civil protection: water, food, storage, medicines.
